pageTitle: KAWSAY — What body will you land with?
pageDescription: KAWSAY — a health copilot that shows astronauts the body they will land with. NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 prototype, not a medical device.

hero.title: KAWSAY
hero.subtitle: A health copilot for astronauts on long missions. It answers the one question no dashboard does: what body will you land with?

video.title: KAWSAY in
video.subtitle: A crew member skips exercise for a week, sees their landing-day self decline, and brings it back.
video.soonHint: Meanwhile, the demo plays the full story of mission day 142 with no data entry.

challenge.title: The Challenge We're
challenge.subtitle: In deep space, the astronaut is their own first doctor

problems.title: Damage is slow and silent
problems.text: Bone and fitness decline a little every day. No single day feels different, so nobody notices the slope.

problems.title: Hazards compound
problems.text: A headache can mean poor sleep, high CO₂, low oxygen or eye pressure. One indicator at a time misses it.

problems.title: Earth is up to 20 minutes away
problems.text: From Mars, every answer takes up to 40 minutes round trip, or never comes during conjunction.

problems.title: Landing hits the weakest body
problems.text: The most demanding day of the mission arrives when the body is at its worst after months without gravity.

solutions.title: Future Self
solutions.text: Shows you today next to your projected self on arrival day. Every workout, glass of water and hour of sleep bends the line.

solutions.title: Compound risk engine
solutions.text: Explainable rules read several indicators together. Each one cites the NASA page behind it.

solutions.title: Earth-independent loop
solutions.text: Measure, understand, act, verify, escalate. KAWSAY checks that the fix worked before it asks Earth.

solutions.title: An alarm on your wrist
solutions.text: The smart band watches six signals around the clock and raises the alarm, even with the app in the background.

technology.title: Powered by
technology.subtitle: Official NASA research, a deterministic engine and a wearable, in an app that never needs a server

items.title: NASA Human Research Program
items.text: The 5 hazards of spaceflight and NASA's risk pages set our rules: bone loss of 1–1.5% a month, fitness, SANS, sleep and hypoxia.

items.title: NASA-STD-3001 limits
items.text: Cabin CO₂ at or under 3 mmHg (1-hour average) drives the headache rule. Every figure is tagged NASA or Prototype.

items.title: Smart band integration
items.text: Heart rate, HRV, blood oxygen, breathing rate, skin temperature and motion. Activity context tells exercise from a real alarm.

items.title: Deterministic rules engine
items.text: Pure TypeScript with unit tests for every function. No AI decides a health status; rules do, and they explain why.

items.title: TypeScript and React 19
items.text: Built with Vite and Tailwind CSS, with Zustand for state, Motion for animation and design tokens from our own design system.

items.title: Offline-first by design
items.text: A Progressive Web App with a local IndexedDB database. Nothing leaves the device, and it keeps working with no signal.

items.title: Windows desktop app
items.text: An Electron build that loads only from disk and blocks every network request. One .exe, ready for the station laptop.

items.title: Communication-delay model
items.text: Knows the one-way delay for the ISS, Orion, the Moon and Mars, and shows when Earth's answer will arrive.

items.title: Vercel and GitHub Actions
items.text: Every change is type-checked, tested and built in CI, then deployed to the public demo.

cta.title: Meet your landing-day self
cta.text: Open the web app in your browser, or download the Windows app and run it with no internet.
